```
date        = year "-" month "-" day
year        = 4DIGIT                           ; 0000 to 9999
            / "-" neg-year                     ; years before 0000
            / "+" NZDIGIT 4*DIGIT              ; years after 9999; no leading zeros
neg-year    = "000" NZDIGIT / "00" NZDIGIT DIGIT / "0" NZDIGIT 2DIGIT
            / NZDIGIT 3*DIGIT                  ; four digits or more, never "0000"
month       = 2DIGIT                           ; 01-12; 00 only under zero_date / incomplete_date
day         = 2DIGIT                           ; 01-31; 00 only under zero_date / incomplete_date
clock       = hour ":" minute ":" second [ "." secfrac ]
hour        = 2DIGIT                           ; 00-23; 24 only under allows_24h with 00:00 and zero fraction
minute      = 2DIGIT                           ; 00-59
second      = 2DIGIT                           ; 00-59
secfrac     = 1*DIGIT                          ; exactly fractional_second_digits digits; absent when 0
offset      = ("+" / "-") 2DIGIT ":" 2DIGIT [ ":" 2DIGIT ]   ; UTC is "+00:00"; "Z" and "-00:00" are forbidden; seconds only when not zero
zone-name   = "[" 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "/" / "_" / "+" / "-" / "." ) "]"
infinite    = "Infinity" / "-Infinity"
```

| `component_set` | `zone_semantics` | Form |
|---|---|---|
| `DATE` | `NONE` | `DQUOTE ( date / infinite ) DQUOTE` |
| `TIME` | `NONE` | `DQUOTE clock DQUOTE` |
| `TIME` | `OFFSET_RETAINED` | `DQUOTE clock offset DQUOTE` |
| `DATETIME` | `NONE` | `DQUOTE ( date "T" clock / infinite ) DQUOTE` |
| `DATETIME` | `UTC_INSTANT` | `DQUOTE ( date "T" clock "+00:00" / infinite ) DQUOTE` |
| `DATETIME` | `OFFSET_RETAINED` | `DQUOTE ( date "T" clock offset / infinite ) DQUOTE` |
| `DATETIME` | `NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED` | `DQUOTE ( date "T" clock offset [zone-name] / infinite ) DQUOTE` |
| `DATETIME` | `SESSION_LOCAL` | `DQUOTE ( date "T" clock "+00:00" / infinite ) DQUOTE` |

Rules:

- **Calendar.** Dates are proleptic Gregorian. Year numbering is astronomical: year `0000` is 1 BCE and `-0044` is 45 BCE. A year below 0001 is admitted only if `bce_years` is true. A year above 9999 is admitted only if `year_max` exceeds 9999.
- **No leap seconds.** `second` is 00 to 59. No supported engine stores a second of 60.
- **No invented components.** A `TIME` value has no date. A `DATETIME` with `zone_semantics: NONE` has no offset.
- **UTC.** The producer writes an instant with `+00:00`. It never writes `Z`.
- **Offset seconds.** An engine that retains an offset specified to the second (PostgreSQL `timetz`) keeps it: the producer writes `:SS` if and only if the seconds are not zero.
- **Named zones.** Under `NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED`, the producer always writes the offset in effect for the value. It appends the zone name, in the bracket syntax of RFC 9557, if and only if the engine stored a zone name for that value. The name is the IANA identifier as the engine stores it.
- **Resolution.** If `resolution` is coarser than the fraction digits, the producer writes the fraction nearest to the stored tick, and the inverse maps the fraction back to the nearest tick. SQL Server `DATETIME` stores ticks of 1/300 second. The producer writes tick `k` within a second as the millisecond nearest to `k` × 1000 / 300, so ticks 0, 1, 2, 3 are `.000`, `.003`, `.007`, `.010`. The written `.003` represents tick 1. It is not a claim of three milliseconds. The inverse recovers `k` as the tick nearest to the written milliseconds × 300 / 1000.
- **Special values** are admitted only under their flags: `0000-00-00` and `0000-00-00T00:00:00` under `zero_date`; a zero month or day under `incomplete_date`; a day that does not exist in its month under `nonexistent_date`; `Infinity` and `-Infinity` under `infinite_date`; `24:00:00` under `allows_24h`.
- **Sentinels are not dates.** A zero or incomplete date is a sentinel. `bce_years`, `year_min` and `year_max` do not apply to it. Under a zoned form it carries the declared fraction digits and the offset `+00:00`: `0000-00-00T00:00:00.000000+00:00`.

Inverse: parse the fields. The descriptor says which components, digits and zone rule apply.

```
"D":   "2026-03-22"                                  // temporal/date
"D":   "-0044-03-15"                                 // 45 BCE, bce_years
"D":   "0000-00-00"                                  // MySQL zero date, zero_date
"T":   "14:30:00.000"                                // temporal/time/NONE/3
"T":   "24:00:00"                                    // allows_24h, 0 digits
"TS":  "2026-03-22T14:30:00"                         // temporal/datetime/NONE/0 (Oracle DATE)
"TS":  "2026-03-22T14:30:00.000000+00:00"            // UTC_INSTANT, 6 digits
"TS":  "2026-03-22T14:30:00.1234567+05:30"           // OFFSET_RETAINED, 7 digits
"TS":  "2026-03-22T10:00:00.000000-04:00[America/New_York]"   // NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED, name stored
"TS":  "2026-03-22T10:00:00.000000-04:00"            // NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED, offset stored
"TS":  "2026-03-22T14:30:00.003"                     // SQL Server DATETIME tick 1
"TS":  "Infinity"                                    // infinite_date
```

## 6.4 Interval form

Form: a JSON object with exactly three members, in this order: `months`, `days`, `seconds`. Each member is a string.

```
interval = "{" DQUOTE "months" DQUOTE ":" int-string ","
               DQUOTE "days"   DQUOTE ":" int-string ","
               DQUOTE "seconds" DQUOTE ":" DQUOTE ["-"] uint ["." secfrac] DQUOTE "}"
```

Rules:

- Under `time_basis: CALENDAR`, the three components are the stored components of the engine. Months and days never convert into each other. The producer folds years into months (one year is twelve months) and folds hours and minutes into seconds.
- Under `time_basis: ELAPSED`, `months` and `days` are `"0"`, and `seconds` carries the whole value.
- `seconds` has exactly `fractional_second_digits` fraction digits. It has no point if that count is zero.
- Each component carries its own sign if the engine allows it. A zero component has no sign.
- The object has no whitespace between tokens, so the value is one string of characters.
- An infinite interval is the string `"Infinity"` or `"-Infinity"` in place of the object, admitted only if the `infinity` flag is true (P-TYPE-9).

Inverse: read the three components, or the special string.

```
"ELAPSED": {"months":"0","days":"0","seconds":"-90000.000000"}      // MySQL TIME(6), -25:00:00
"AGE":     {"months":"14","days":"-2","seconds":"3.500000"}         // PostgreSQL interval
"TENURE":  {"months":"26","days":"0","seconds":"0"}                 // Oracle INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH '2-2'
"RUN":     {"months":"0","days":"0","seconds":"189015.123456"}      // Oracle INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND '2 04:30:15.123456'
```

## 6.5 Collection forms

### 6.5.1 array

Form: one of two. The plain form is nested JSON arrays, one level per dimension, each element in the form of its element type. The shaped form is a JSON object with three members: `shape` (the extent of each dimension), `lower_bounds` (the lower bound of each dimension) and `elements` (the elements, flat, in row-major order).

```
array-plain  = "[" [ item *( "," item ) ] "]"
item         = form / "null" / array-plain               ; array-plain for the next dimension
array-shaped = "{" DQUOTE "shape" DQUOTE ":" "[" uint *( "," uint ) "]" ","
                   DQUOTE "lower_bounds" DQUOTE ":" "[" sint *( "," sint ) "]" ","
                   DQUOTE "elements" DQUOTE ":" "[" [ elem *( "," elem ) ] "]" "}"
elem         = form / "null"
```

Rules: the producer uses the plain form if and only if three conditions hold. The element's base value form is never a JSON array. So the element type is not `array`, `map`, a multi-select `enumeration`, or a `vector` whose form is a JSON array (Section 6.6.2). Every lower bound is one. Either the value has one dimension, or no dimension has an extent of zero. In every other case it uses the shaped form. There, `shape` makes the inverse unique, even when the element's form is a JSON array or a dimension is empty. `lower_bounds` has the same length as `shape`. A value is rectangular: every row of a dimension has the same extent. A null element is `null`. An empty one-dimensional array, and an engine's empty array with no dimensions, is `[]`. A multidimensional array with an empty dimension is shaped: `{"shape":[0,3],"lower_bounds":[1,1],"elements":[]}`. Inverse: in the plain form, read the shape from the nesting; in the shaped form, read `shape` and `lower_bounds` and fold `elements` in row-major order. The product of `shape` equals the length of `elements`.

```
"TAGS":   ["temperature","pressure",null]
"GRID":   [[1,2],[3,4]]
"OFFSET": {"shape":[3],"lower_bounds":[0],"elements":[10,20,30]}      // PostgreSQL '[0:2]={10,20,30}'
"NESTED": {"shape":[1],"lower_bounds":[1],"elements":[[1]]}          // one element, itself the array [1]
"ATTRS":  {"shape":[2],"lower_bounds":[1],"elements":[[{"key":"a","value":"1"}],[]]}   // array of map
```

### 6.5.2 map

Form: a JSON array of entry objects. Each entry has exactly two members, `key` then `value`, each in the form of its type.

```
map     = "[" [ entry *( "," entry ) ] "]"
entry   = "{" DQUOTE "key" DQUOTE ":" form "," DQUOTE "value" DQUOTE ":" ( form / "null" ) "}"
```

Rules: the entries are in ascending order of the key, whatever order the engine returns them in. Keys are compared as UTF-8 bytes of the decoded key: the characters of a string key after JSON unescaping, or the JSON text of any other key. A key that holds a tab sorts by the byte 0x09, not by its escape `\t`. No key appears twice. An empty map is `[]`. Inverse: read the entries.

```
"PROPS": [{"key":"color","value":"red"},{"key":"size","value":null}]        // keys in UTF-8 byte order
```

### 6.5.3 struct

Form: a JSON object with one member per field, in the declared field order, each in the form of its field. Every field is present. A null field is `null`. There are no other members.

```
struct = "{" member *( "," member ) "}"
member = json-string ":" ( form / "null" )
```

Inverse: read the members by name. The order is checked, not inferred.

```
"HOME": {"street":"1 Main St","zip":27601}
```

## 6.6 Spatial, vector, range, identifier and network forms

### 6.6.1 spatial

Form: a JSON string that holds `SRID=`, the SRID, `;`, and then Well-Known Text per OGC 06-103r4, restricted as follows.

```
ewkt       = DQUOTE "SRID=" uint ";" wkt DQUOTE
wkt        = tag ( "(" body ")" / " EMPTY" / " " dim " " ( "(" body ")" / "EMPTY" ) )
tag        = "POINT" / "LINESTRING" / "POLYGON" / "MULTIPOINT" / "MULTILINESTRING" / "MULTIPOLYGON"
           / "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION" / "CIRCULARSTRING" / "COMPOUNDCURVE" / "CURVEPOLYGON"
           / "MULTICURVE" / "MULTISURFACE" / "POLYHEDRALSURFACE" / "TIN" / "TRIANGLE"
dim        = "Z" / "M" / "ZM"
body       = <the production for the tag in OGC 06-103r4 Section 7, with
              coordinate below as its number, and the spacing rules below>
coordinate = plain / exp / "-0"                 ; ordinate_kind BINARY64: the binary64 number form of Section 6.2.4, and "-0"
           / "NaN" / "Infinity" / "-Infinity"     ; BINARY64 only, under the ordinate_specials flag
           / ["-"] finite                         ; ordinate_kind DECIMAL: the finite scientific string of Section 6.2.3, signed, unquoted
```

Rules: the SRID prefix is always present, and it is `SRID=0` if the SRID is unknown. Tags are upper-case. Without a dimension marker, `(` follows the tag with no space, and `EMPTY` follows it after one space. With a dimension marker, one space separates the tag from the marker, and one space separates the marker from `(` or `EMPTY`. One space separates ordinates. A comma with no space separates points. Under `ordinate_kind: BINARY64`, ordinates use the binary64 number form of Section 6.2.4; its lower-case `e` exponent is an extension of OGC 06-103r4, which writes `E`. Under `ordinate_kind: DECIMAL`, ordinates use the finite scientific-string form of Section 6.2.3, with its sign and without quotation marks, so that an exact ordinate such as `-9007199254740993` keeps every digit. Under `BINARY64`, a negative zero ordinate is written `-0`. `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity` are written as those tokens when the `ordinate_specials` flag is true. The tokens are inside the EWKT string, so the number rules of Section 6.1 do not apply to them. Under `DECIMAL`, a zero ordinate has no sign. The two ordinate grammars are selected by the trait; they are not alternatives within one value. Longitude or x comes first. This is the form the producer writes. It is not the engine's own text output, which differs in spacing and dimension markers. Inverse: parse the WKT.

```
"LOCATION": "SRID=4326;POINT(-73.9857 40.7484)"
"PATH":     "SRID=3857;LINESTRING(0 0,10 10,20 0)"
"SOLID":    "SRID=0;POINT Z (1 2 3)"
"NONE":     "SRID=4326;POINT EMPTY"
```

### 6.6.2 vector

| Deciding trait | Form |
|---|---|
| `element_type` fixed, not `BINARY`, `sparse: false` | JSON array of elements, each in its element form |
| `element_type: BINARY`, `dimension` fixed | Base64 string of the packed bits |
| `element_type: BINARY`, `dimension: null` | JSON object `{"dimension":n,"bits":"..."}` |
| `element_type` fixed, `sparse: true` | JSON object `{"dimension":n,"indices":[...],"values":[...]}` |
| `element_type: null`, `sparse: false` | JSON object `{"format":"FLOAT32","values":[...]}`, or `{"format":"BINARY","dimension":n,"bits":"..."}` |
| `element_type: null`, `sparse: true` | JSON object `{"format":"FLOAT32","dimension":n,"indices":[...],"values":[...]}`; `format` is never `BINARY` |

The six cases are exclusive and cover every valid combination. `format` is one of the five element types.

```
vec-dense      = "[" [ vec-elem *( "," vec-elem ) ] "]"
vec-bits       = base64
vec-bits-obj   = "{" DQUOTE "dimension" DQUOTE ":" uint "," DQUOTE "bits" DQUOTE ":" base64 "}"
vec-sparse     = "{" DQUOTE "dimension" DQUOTE ":" uint "," indices "," values "}"
vec-any        = "{" DQUOTE "format" DQUOTE ":" num-format "," values "}"
               / "{" DQUOTE "format" DQUOTE ":" DQUOTE "BINARY" DQUOTE ","
                     DQUOTE "dimension" DQUOTE ":" uint "," DQUOTE "bits" DQUOTE ":" base64 "}"
vec-any-sparse = "{" DQUOTE "format" DQUOTE ":" num-format ","
                     DQUOTE "dimension" DQUOTE ":" uint "," indices "," values "}"
indices        = DQUOTE "indices" DQUOTE ":" "[" [ uint *( "," uint ) ] "]"
values         = DQUOTE "values" DQUOTE ":" "[" [ vec-elem *( "," vec-elem ) ] "]"
num-format     = DQUOTE ( "FLOAT16" / "FLOAT32" / "FLOAT64" / "INT8" ) DQUOTE
vec-elem       = plain / exp / "-0"          ; FLOAT formats: Section 6.2.4, and "-0"; INT8: sint
```

Element forms: `FLOAT16`, `FLOAT32` and `FLOAT64` use the binary float number form of Section 6.2.4 against that format (binary16 for `FLOAT16`). `INT8` uses the integer number form. `BINARY` is one bit per element: the producer packs the bits most significant bit first, zero-pads the final byte, and writes the whole vector as one Base64 string. In the sparse form, `indices` are zero-based and ascending (one less than an engine's one-based index), `values` has the same length, and only non-zero elements appear. Under `element_type: null`, `format` names the per-value format, so two values with equal elements in different formats differ on the wire; a sparse value under `element_type: null` never has `format: BINARY`. A negative zero element is written `-0`; the token is inside a JSON array that the binding defines, so the number rule of Section 6.1 does not apply to it. Inverse: read the elements. For `BINARY`, the significant bit count is the descriptor's `dimension` when fixed, and the value's `dimension` member otherwise.

```
"EMB":   [0.023,-0.184,0.762]
"BITS":  "sAA="                                           // BINARY, dimension 10: 1011000000 packed as B0 00
"SPARSE": {"dimension":1536,"indices":[3,900],"values":[0.5,-0.25]}
```

### 6.6.3 range

Form: a JSON object with exactly five members, in this order: `lower`, `upper`, `lower_inclusive`, `upper_inclusive`, `empty`.

```
range = "{" DQUOTE "lower" DQUOTE ":" ( form / "null" ) ","
            DQUOTE "upper" DQUOTE ":" ( form / "null" ) ","
            DQUOTE "lower_inclusive" DQUOTE ":" bool ","
            DQUOTE "upper_inclusive" DQUOTE ":" bool ","
            DQUOTE "empty" DQUOTE ":" bool "}"
```

Rules: a bound is in the form of the element type. An unbounded side has `null` and `false`. The empty range has both bounds `null`, both flags `false`, and `empty` `true`. A bound of `"Infinity"` or `"-Infinity"` is admitted only if the range's `infinity` flag is true. The producer writes the bounds as the engine stores them after its own canonicalization. Inverse: read the members.

```
"VALID": {"lower":"0.5","upper":"2.5","lower_inclusive":true,"upper_inclusive":false,"empty":false}
"OPEN":  {"lower":null,"upper":10,"lower_inclusive":false,"upper_inclusive":false,"empty":false}
"NONE":  {"lower":null,"upper":null,"lower_inclusive":false,"upper_inclusive":false,"empty":true}
```

### 6.6.4 identifier

Form: a JSON string that holds the engine's canonical character form of the identity, as the dictionary rule names it. The dictionary rule names the function that produces the characters and their length. Inverse: the string.

```
identifier = json-string                    ; content as the dictionary rule names it
```

```
"RID": "AAAR3sAAEAAAACXAAA"        // Oracle ROWID, 18 characters
```

### 6.6.5 network

| `address_family` | Form |
|---|---|
| `INET`, `CIDR` | JSON string: address, `/`, prefix length |
| `MAC` | JSON string: octets as lower-case hexadecimal pairs separated by `:` |

```
ipv4      = DQUOTE dec-octet 3( "." dec-octet ) "/" uint DQUOTE      ; dec-octet without leading zeros; prefix 0-32
ipv6      = DQUOTE rfc5952-address "/" uint DQUOTE                    ; prefix 0-128
mac       = DQUOTE 2HEXLOWER 5( ":" 2HEXLOWER ) DQUOTE                ; octets 6
mac8      = DQUOTE 2HEXLOWER 7( ":" 2HEXLOWER ) DQUOTE                ; octets 8
```

Rules: the producer always writes the prefix length, so a host address is `/32` or `/128`. IPv6 text follows RFC 5952 Section 4 only: lower-case, longest zero run compressed, no leading zeros in a group, and no embedded-IPv4 notation (`::ffff:c000:201`, not `::ffff:192.0.2.1`, whatever the engine prints). For `CIDR`, the host bits are zero. Inverse: parse the address and the prefix.

```
"CLIENT": "192.168.10.5/32"
"NET":    "10.0.0.0/8"
"V6":     "2001:db8::1/128"
"HW":     "08:00:2b:01:02:03"
```

## 6.7 NATIVE forms

| `carrier` | Form |
|---|---|
| `text` | JSON string holding the characters the codec produces, escaped per Section 6.9 |
| `binary` | JSON string holding the Base64 encoding of the bytes the codec produces, per Section 6.10 |

The codec's grammar governs the content. Inverse: the codec's inverse.

```
"ORG_NODE": "/1/2/3/"                          // sqlserver.hierarchyid.path@1, text
"UDT_RAW":  "AQIDBA=="                         // a binary carrier
```

## 6.8 Special values

A capability flag in the descriptor announces each special value. Each special value has one spelling. A producer MUST NOT emit a special value if its flag is not true (P-TYPE-9).

| Flag | Family | Spelling |
|---|---|---|
| `nan` | decimal | `"NaN"`; also `"-NaN"` under `DECIMAL_FLOAT` |
| `signaling_nan` | decimal | `"sNaN"`; also `"-sNaN"` under `DECIMAL_FLOAT` |
| `infinity` | decimal | `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"` |
| `signed_zero` | decimal, `BINARY_FLOAT` | `"-0"` |
| `signed_zero` | decimal, other kinds | the sign is kept and the exponent is kept: `"-0.00"`, `"-0E+3"` |
| `infinite_date` | temporal | `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"` |
| `infinity` | interval | `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`, in place of the component object |
| `zero_date` | temporal | `"0000-00-00"`, or `"0000-00-00T"` followed by the stored clock (MySQL stores `0000-00-00 12:34:56`), with the declared fraction digits and, under a zoned form, `+00:00` |
| `nonexistent_date` | temporal | the stored digits, for example `"2026-04-31"` |
| `incomplete_date` | temporal | the stored digits, for example `"2026-00-15"` |
| `allows_24h` | temporal | `"24:00:00"`, with the declared fraction digits as zeros |
| `error_value` | enumeration | `0` (a JSON number) |
| `bce_years` | temporal | a signed year: `"-0044-03-15"` |
| `infinity` | range | a bound of `"Infinity"` or `"-Infinity"` |

The producer never converts a special value to null, and never converts it to a nearby ordinary value.

## 6.9 Working with Control Characters in JSON

### 6.9.1 The problem

A `string`, `document`, `enumeration` label or NATIVE text value can contain any Unicode character that the source engine stored, including control characters. JSON requires an escape for some of them, and permits several escape spellings for each. Two producers that pick different spellings emit different bytes for the same value. That defeats byte comparison and hashing. This section fixes one spelling.

### 6.9.2 Rules

1. **Escape only what RFC 8259 requires.** The producer escapes the characters U+0000 to U+001F, the quotation mark U+0022, and the reverse solidus U+005C. It writes every other character as its UTF-8 bytes, including U+007F and every character above U+007F. It does not escape the solidus U+002F.
2. **Short escapes where they exist.** U+0008 is `\b`, U+0009 is `\t`, U+000A is `\n`, U+000C is `\f`, U+000D is `\r`, U+0022 is `\"`, U+005C is `\\`.
3. **Four-digit lower-case escapes for the rest.** For every other character in U+0000 to U+001F, the producer writes `\u` and four lower-case hexadecimal digits: U+0000 is `\u0000`, and U+001B is `\u001b`.
4. **No other escapes.** Every character above U+001F, except U+0022 and U+005C, is written directly. `\u00e9` for é, `\u2028` for the line separator, and surrogate-pair escapes for characters above U+FFFF are forbidden. The producer writes the characters directly.
5. **Valid Unicode only.** A value is a sequence of Unicode scalar values. A lone surrogate has no spelling. A source value that is not valid Unicode is a decode failure under Section 6.11.
6. **Nothing is dropped or replaced.** A control character in the source is a character of the value. The producer writes U+0000 as `\u0000`. It writes the trailing spaces of a `fixed` string.

```
json-string = DQUOTE *jchar DQUOTE
jchar       = unescaped / short-escape / u-escape
unescaped   = %x20-21 / %x23-5B / %x5D-D7FF / %xE000-10FFFF      ; no surrogate code points
short-escape= "\" ( %x22 / %x5C / "b" / "f" / "n" / "r" / "t" )
u-escape    = "\u00" ( "0" ( %x30-37 / "b" / "e" / "f" ) / "1" HEXLOWER )
                                                    ; U+0000 to U+001F without a short escape
```

### 6.9.3 Worked examples

A VARCHAR value that contains a tab, a newline and a quotation mark.

```
Source characters:   Line one<TAB>col<LF>He said "hi"
Row event:           "NOTE": "Line one\tcol\nHe said \"hi\""
```

A value that contains a NUL character and an escape character (U+001B).

```
Source characters:   AB<NUL>CD<ESC>[0m
Row event:           "RAW_TEXT": "AB\u0000CD\u001b[0m"
```

A value with non-ASCII characters. The producer escapes nothing. It writes the UTF-8 bytes.

```
Source characters:   Café ☕ 😀
Row event:           "TITLE": "Café ☕ 😀"
Bytes:               43 61 66 C3 A9 20 E2 98 95 20 F0 9F 98 80
```

A CHAR(8) value with trailing padding. The padding is part of the value.

```
Source value:        "AB      " (two letters, six spaces)
Descriptor:          "fixed": true, "max_length": 8
Row event:           "CODE": "AB      "
```

A JSON document column. The document is a string, so the producer escapes its quotation marks once. It does not escape the content again.

```
Stored document:     {"a": "x\ty"}         (the stored text contains a backslash-t escape, not a tab)
Row event:           "DOC": "{\"a\": \"x\\ty\"}"
```

A line separator U+2028. Some JavaScript environments once rejected it unescaped. RFC 8259 permits it, and this binding writes it directly.

```
Source characters:   first<U+2028>second
Row event:           "TXT": "first<U+2028>second"      (shown symbolically; the wire holds the bytes E2 80 A8, not an escape)
```

## 6.10 Byte Encoding in JSON

### 6.10.1 Rules

Bytes have no JSON form of their own. Three kinds of value are bytes: a `binary` family value, a NATIVE value with a `binary` carrier, and a packed `BINARY` vector. The producer writes each one as a JSON string that holds the Base64 encoding of the bytes.

1. **Alphabet.** The standard alphabet of RFC 4648 Section 4: `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `+`, `/`. The URL-safe alphabet (`-`, `_`) is forbidden.
2. **Padding.** The producer pads the output with `=` to a multiple of four characters. Unpadded output is forbidden.
3. **Canonical.** The bits that padding covers are zero. An encoding with non-zero trailing bits is outside the grammar, because two different strings would otherwise decode to the same bytes.
4. **No whitespace.** The string contains no line breaks, spaces or other characters.
5. **Empty.** The producer writes zero bytes as `""`.
6. **Fixed length.** For `fixed: true`, the bytes include the engine's padding to `max_length_bytes`, so the Base64 length is the same for every value.

```
base64  = DQUOTE *( 4b64 ) [ b64 b64-z4 "==" / 2b64 b64-z2 "=" ] DQUOTE
b64     = ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "/"
b64-z4  = "A" / "Q" / "g" / "w"                   ; low four bits zero
b64-z2  = "A" / "E" / "I" / "M" / "Q" / "U" / "Y" / "c"
        / "g" / "k" / "o" / "s" / "w" / "0" / "4" / "8"   ; low two bits zero
```

Inverse: Base64 decoding. Input outside the grammar has no inverse.

### 6.10.2 Worked examples

| Bytes (hex) | Length | Row event |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | 0 | `""` |
| `00` | 1 | `"AA=="` |
| `FF` | 1 | `"/w=="` |
| `DE AD` | 2 | `"3q0="` |
| `DE AD BE` | 3 | `"3q2+"` |
| `DE AD BE EF` | 4 | `"3q2+7w=="` |
| `00 00 00 00 00 00 07 D2` | 8 | `"AAAAAAAAB9I="` |

A SQL Server `ROWVERSION` (eight bytes, `binary/fixed`), two consecutive values.

```
"ROW_VER": "AAAAAAAAB9I="        // 0x00000000000007D2
"ROW_VER": "AAAAAAAAB9M="        // 0x00000000000007D3
```

A `BINARY(4)` column holding two bytes. The engine pads to four; the padding bytes are part of the value.

```
Stored bytes:  AB CD 00 00
Row event:     "KEY4": "q80AAA=="
```

A `BINARY` vector of ten bits `1011000000`, packed MSB first into two bytes `B0 00`.

```
"BITS": "sAA="
```

Strings outside the grammar. `"3q2+7w"` lacks padding. `"3q0"` has a wrong length. `"3q1="` has a non-zero trailing bit; the canonical encoding of `DE AD` is `"3q0="`. None of the three is a value of the form. A producer that writes one is non-conformant.

A binary column that holds text in a character set that the dictionary carries as bytes (Section 6.11). The bytes are the stored bytes. The descriptor says what they are.

```
Descriptor:    "logical_type": "binary", "parameters": { ..., "charset": "cp932" }
Stored bytes:  93 FA 96 7B 8C EA
Row event:     "NAME_JP": "k/qWe4zq"
```

## 6.11 Character sets

JSON strings are Unicode. For most source character sets, the conversion to Unicode is one-to-one and loses nothing. For a few, two source code points map to one Unicode character, so the original bytes cannot be recovered from the Unicode text. This section keeps that case explicit and small.

**Default.** A character column is `string`. The producer converts its values to Unicode with no normalization. The `charset` trait records the source character set.

**Character sets carried as bytes.** Section 7.10 lists the character sets whose conversion is not one-to-one. Every column in one of those character sets is `binary` with the `charset` trait, not `string`. The original bytes survive. A consumer with a character set library can decode them.

**Who decides.** The dictionary decides, per character set. The producer does not decide per value.

**Strings inside other families.** The same rule applies to a string nested in an `array`, `map`, `struct` or `range`: its nested descriptor is `binary` with the `charset` trait. A `document`, an `enumeration` label and a NATIVE text value have no byte-carried form. Such a value in a character set of Section 7.10 cannot be written at full fidelity. The producer names the column in the unavailable-value report (Section 2).

**Invalid bytes.** A value in a one-to-one character set that is not valid in that character set is a decode failure. Validity is judged by the engine's own conversion. A byte the engine maps to a character is valid; SQL Server maps the undefined bytes of cp1252, such as 0x81, to U+0081. The producer MUST NOT emit a replacement character and MUST NOT drop bytes (P-TYPE-4). It names the column in the unavailable-value report for that image (P-TYPE-4).

**Character lengths of byte-carried columns.** A column in a byte-carried character set of Section 7.10 can be declared with character length semantics. Its `binary` descriptor then has `max_length_bytes` equal to the character length times the character set's maximum bytes per character, as an upper bound. `fixed` describes bytes, not characters: it is true only when every value of the column has exactly `max_length_bytes` bytes. A fixed-character column in a variable-width character set has `fixed: false`, because its padded values differ in byte length (Oracle `CHAR(2 CHAR)` under `JA16SJIS` stores 2, 3 or 4 bytes). The producer carries the stored bytes, padding included, and adds none. `attributes.length_semantics_source` and `source_type` keep the character declaration.

**Unpaired surrogates.** An engine that stores UTF-16 code units can hold an unpaired surrogate (SQL Server `NVARCHAR`, Oracle `AL16UTF16`, MySQL `utf16`). Such a value is not a sequence of Unicode scalar values. It is a decode failure under Section 6.9.2 rule 5.

**Out of scope.** Collation and lexical normalization of documents.

Worked example: a MySQL `VARCHAR(50) CHARACTER SET cp932` column and a MySQL `VARCHAR(50) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4` column that hold the same Japanese name.

```
cp932 column:    "logical_type": "binary", "parameters": { "max_length_bytes": 100, "fixed": false, "lob": false, "charset": "cp932" }
                 "NAME_JP": "k/qWe4zq"                     // bytes 93 FA 96 7B 8C EA

utf8mb4 column:  "logical_type": "string", "parameters": { "max_length": 50, "length_unit": "CODE_POINT", "fixed": false, "charset": "utf8mb4", "lob": false }
                 "NAME_JP": "日本語"
```

## 6.12 Worked examples

The examples show the `data` block of an event, or its `columns[]` array, and omit the CloudEvents envelope and the `json_schema` member. They are fragments, not complete events.

### 6.12.1 Oracle Database: OBJECT_METADATA then INSERT

```
// OBJECT_METADATA (data block; envelope omitted)
"data": {
  "table": { "catalog": "ORCL", "schema": "FINANCE", "name": "FIN_TRANSACTIONS" },
  "schema_version": 1,
  "primary_key": ["TXN_ID"],
  "columns": [
    { "name": "TXN_ID",      "ordinal": 1, "source_type": "NUMBER(19,0)",
      "logical_type": "decimal",
      "parameters": { "representation_kind": "FIXED_DECIMAL", "precision": 19, "scale": 0 },
      "nullable": false, "pk": true },
    { "name": "AMOUNT",      "ordinal": 2, "source_type": "NUMBER(15,2)",
      "logical_type": "decimal",
      "parameters": { "representation_kind": "FIXED_DECIMAL", "precision": 15, "scale": 2 },
      "nullable": false, "pk": false },
    { "name": "MAGNITUDE",   "ordinal": 3, "source_type": "NUMBER(20,-2)",
      "logical_type": "decimal",
      "parameters": { "representation_kind": "FIXED_DECIMAL", "precision": 20, "scale": -2 },
      "nullable": true, "pk": false },
    { "name": "RATIO",       "ordinal": 4, "source_type": "NUMBER",
      "logical_type": "decimal",
      "parameters": { "representation_kind": "VARIABLE_DECIMAL", "precision": null },
      "nullable": true, "pk": false },
    { "name": "POSTED_DATE", "ordinal": 5, "source_type": "DATE",
      "logical_type": "temporal",
      "parameters": { "component_set": "DATETIME", "fractional_second_digits": 0, "resolution": null,
                      "zone_semantics": "NONE", "year_min": -4712, "year_max": 9999, "bce_years": true },
      "nullable": false, "pk": false },
    { "name": "SETTLED_TS",  "ordinal": 6, "source_type": "TIMESTAMP(9) WITH TIME ZONE",
      "logical_type": "temporal",
      "parameters": { "component_set": "DATETIME", "fractional_second_digits": 9, "resolution": null,
                      "zone_semantics": "NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED", "year_min": -4712, "year_max": 9999, "bce_years": true },
      "nullable": true, "pk": false },
    { "name": "NOTES",       "ordinal": 7, "source_type": "CLOB",
      "logical_type": "string",
      "parameters": { "max_length": null, "length_unit": "CODE_POINT", "fixed": false,
                      "charset": "AL32UTF8", "lob": true },
      "nullable": true, "pk": false },
    { "name": "ATTACHMENT",  "ordinal": 8, "source_type": "BLOB",
      "logical_type": "binary",
      "parameters": { "max_length_bytes": null, "fixed": false, "lob": true, "charset": null },
      "nullable": true, "pk": false },
    { "name": "RID",         "ordinal": 9, "source_type": "ROWID",
      "logical_type": "identifier",
      "parameters": { "identity_kind": "ROWID", "stable": false },
      "nullable": false, "pk": false }
  ]
}

// INSERT (data block)
"data": {
  "table": { "catalog": "ORCL", "schema": "FINANCE", "name": "FIN_TRANSACTIONS" },
  "primary_key": ["TXN_ID"],
  "before": null,
  "after": {
    "TXN_ID":      "8675309000001",
    "AMOUNT":      "1250000.00",
    "MAGNITUDE":   "134500",
    "RATIO":       "0.6180339887",
    "POSTED_DATE": "2026-03-22T14:30:00",
    "SETTLED_TS":  "2026-03-22T14:30:00.123456789+05:30",
    "NOTES":       "Wire ref:\tWR-2026-0042\nApproved.",
    "ATTACHMENT":  null,
    "RID":         "AAAR3sAAEAAAACXAAA"
  },
  "_null_columns": [],
  "_lob_overflow": ["ATTACHMENT"]

```

`TXN_ID` is a fixed decimal with scale 0, so it is a digit string with no point. `MAGNITUDE` is 1345 hundreds. `NOTES` contains a tab and a newline, escaped with the short forms. The engine did not supply the LOB content of `ATTACHMENT`. The Specification's `_lob_overflow` says so, and the value is `null`. (A value the producer cannot write at full fidelity goes in the unavailable-value report instead, Section 2.)

# 7. Type Mapping Dictionary

## 7.1 What a dictionary rule is

The dictionary is part of this document. It holds one rule per native type pattern of each supported engine. A rule assigns a family and a trait bundle, or NATIVE with a carrier and a codec. Conformance with this document includes conformance with the dictionary. A conformance checker tests dictionary rules and flags violations.

A rule has these fields.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | A stable identifier, `<engine>.<type>.<n>`. Never reused. |
| `engine` | The engine token. |
| `versions` | The engine version range the rule covers. Default: the version that the rule's table names, and later versions. |
| `native` | The native type pattern. Type names match without regard to case or surrounding whitespace; parameters in the pattern (`p`, `s`, `n`, `fsp`) bind to the declared values. |
| `logical_type` | The family, or `NATIVE`. |
| `parameters` | The trait bundle, with pattern parameters substituted; for NATIVE, the carrier and the codec. |
| `attributes` | Attributes the rule sets, if any. |
| `status` | `active` or `deprecated`. A deprecated rule still governs streams of the wire protocol versions it was active for. |
| `vectors` | The test vectors that prove the rule. |

A rule matches by engine, version and native pattern. Within one applicable rule set, exactly one rule applies to a source type. A table can mark a rule as an exception to a general rule of the same table. The exception matches a narrower pattern, for example an `ENUM` with a duplicate label. Where both match, the exception applies and the general rule does not. Two rules that both match without that relation are a dictionary error. Each table in Sections 7.4 to 7.8 names the engine version it was written against. Their rules cover that version and later versions, until a later rule says otherwise. A rule covers an earlier version only if it names that version. A rule matches the resolved catalog identity of the type, not the spelling of `source_type`. The producer resolves aliases, omitted defaults and modifiers through the engine's catalog. A user-defined type never matches a built-in pattern because its name resembles one. Some rules depend on a database, session or column setting. The table lists each such setting, where the descriptor records it, and which rules use it. The checker tests each rule against the recorded setting.

| Setting | Recorded in | Rules that use it |
|---|---|---|
| Length semantics (Oracle `CHAR_USED`; Db2 string units) | `length_unit`, and `attributes.length_semantics_source` | Oracle `CHAR`, `VARCHAR2`; Db2 `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `CLOB`, `GRAPHIC`, `VARGRAPHIC`, `DBCLOB` |
| Character set (database, national or column) | `charset` | Every character row; Section 7.10 |
| Collation | `attributes.collation` (always), and for SQL Server also `charset` (the collation's code page) | Every character, enumeration and document row of MySQL and SQL Server; PostgreSQL and Db2 columns with a non-default collation; `sqlserver.sql_variant.typed-json@1` |
| ANSI padding (SQL Server `is_ansi_padded`) | `attributes.ansi_padded` | SQL Server `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `BINARY`, `VARBINARY` |
| SRID | `srid`, or `attributes.srid_per_value` | Every spatial row |
| Monetary locale (PostgreSQL `lc_monetary`) | `attributes.locale` | PostgreSQL `money` |
| Database time zone (Oracle `DBTIMEZONE`) | Not recorded; it changes no descriptor | Oracle `TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE`: the producer reads it to convert each value to an instant |

The tables in Sections 7.4 to 7.8 and 7.13 are the dictionary in readable form. The machine-readable form, `dictionary/type-mappings.yaml`, holds the same rules with their identifiers and vectors, and is kept in step with these tables.

## 7.2 Rule stability and wire protocol versions

- **Published rules do not change.** A correction, a promotion from NATIVE to a family, or a demotion is a new rule with a new identifier.
- **No dictionary version travels in the stream.** Each wire protocol version pins the set of rules that are mandatory for it, as recorded in `versions.yaml`. The `cdcspecversion` on every event is enough to know which rules apply.
- **Adding a rule needs no wire protocol change.** A producer MAY adopt a new rule at once. The rule becomes mandatory at the next wire protocol version.
- **A replacement rule takes effect at a wire protocol version boundary.** A consumer has only the wire protocol version to tell a rule from its replacement. Until the boundary, the earlier rule governs.
- **A producer is judged against the rules of the wire protocol version it declares.** A later rule does not make an earlier producer non-conformant.
- **A consumer never needs the adoption state.** A column mapped by a newly added rule carries its full descriptor, so a consumer decodes it without knowing whether the rule was mandatory or optional for the producer's wire protocol version. For the conformance checker, a column is listed if its rule is in the producer's applicable rule set (Section 2). A producer that has not adopted an optional rule may continue with its unlisted codec until the rule becomes mandatory at the next wire protocol version; the checker judges `listed: false` against that same set.
- **Schema changes are transitive.** A change to anything that a descriptor depends on is an emission schema change: a nested descriptor, an enumeration's labels or order, a composite or object type's attributes, a domain's base type, or a setting that a rule depends on (Section 7.1). The producer emits a new OBJECT_METADATA before the first DML that the change affects.
- **A changed mapping is a schema change.** If the rule for a column changes under a producer, the descriptor of the column changes. The producer then emits a new OBJECT_METADATA before any DML under the new descriptor, as the Specification requires for every emission schema change.

## 7.3 Notation for the engine tables

Each row names a native type pattern and its rule. Trait bundles are abbreviated:

- `integer/<w>/<s>`: `bit_width` w, `signed` s; `min`/`max` null unless shown.
- `fixed(p,s)`, `variable(p)`, `decfloat(p)`, `binary(32|64)`: the `decimal` kinds with their traits.
- `string(n,UNIT)`, `binary(n)`: `max_length` or `max_length_bytes` n, `length_unit`; `fixed`, `lob` and `charset` as shown. `cs:db` means the database character set; `cs:ncs` the national character set; `cs:col` the column's declared character set.
- `datetime/<zone>/<d>`, `date`, `time/<zone>/<d>`: the `temporal` traits; `res` is `resolution`; `years` is `year_min..year_max`.
- `interval/<parts>/<basis>/<d>`.
- Flags are listed by name when true.
- `NATIVE text <codec>` or `NATIVE binary <codec>`.
- A row that marks itself as an exception to a general row takes precedence over it (Section 7.1).

**Defaults.** A row shows every trait whose value differs from its default. A trait that a row does not show has its default: a trait whose type admits null is null; any other boolean trait is false; `bit_order` is `MSB_FIRST`. The descriptor that a producer emits still states every applicable trait (Section 3.2).

## 7.4 Oracle Database

Written against Oracle Database 26ai (version 23.26). The rules cover that version and later versions (Section 7.1).

| Native type pattern | Family and traits | Flags | Attributes and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NUMBER(p,s)`, s ≥ 0 | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | infinity | The engine stores positive and negative infinity in every `NUMBER` column. |
| `NUMBER(p,s)`, s < 0 | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | | Values are multiples of 10^-s. |
| `NUMBER(p)` | decimal `fixed(p,0)` | | |
| `NUMBER`, `NUMBER(*)` | decimal `variable(null)` | infinity | No invented precision. The engine stores positive and negative infinity (displayed `~` and `-~`). The engine stores no trailing zeros, so the coefficient has none. |
| `NUMBER(*,s)` | decimal `fixed(38,s)` | | Oracle resolves `INTEGER`, `INT` and `SMALLINT` to this pattern with s = 0 (`NUMBER(*,0)`), so they match this row. |
| `NUMERIC(p,s)`, `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `DEC(p,s)` | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | | |
| `FLOAT(b)`, `FLOAT`, `REAL`, `DOUBLE PRECISION` | decimal `variable(null)` | | Stored as `NUMBER` with binary precision; not IEEE. |
| `BINARY_FLOAT` | decimal `binary(32)` | nan, infinity, signed_zero | |
| `BINARY_DOUBLE` | decimal `binary(64)` | nan, infinity, signed_zero | |
| `CHAR(n BYTE)`, `CHAR(n)` under BYTE semantics | string `string(n,BYTE)` fixed, cs:db | | `length_semantics_source: "BYTE"` |
| `CHAR(n CHAR)`, `CHAR(n)` under CHAR semantics | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)` fixed, cs:db | | `length_semantics_source: "CHAR"` |
| `VARCHAR2(n BYTE)`, `VARCHAR(n BYTE)`, `VARCHAR2(n)` under BYTE semantics | string `string(n,BYTE)`, cs:db | | `length_semantics_source: "BYTE"` |
| `VARCHAR2(n CHAR)`, `VARCHAR(n CHAR)`, `VARCHAR2(n)` under CHAR semantics | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)`, cs:db | | `length_semantics_source: "CHAR"` |
| `NCHAR(n)` | string `string(n,UTF16_UNIT)` fixed, cs:ncs | | `UTF16_UNIT` under both national character sets: Oracle `UTF8` is CESU-8 and counts a supplementary character as two units, as `AL16UTF16` does. |
| `NVARCHAR2(n)` | string `string(n,UTF16_UNIT)`, cs:ncs | | As above. |
| `CLOB` | string `string(null,CODE_POINT)` lob, cs:db | | Always `string`, even in a character set of Section 7.10: the engine stores a CLOB in `AL16UTF16` when the database character set is varying-width, so the stored data is Unicode. |
| `NCLOB` | string `string(null,UTF16_UNIT)` lob, cs:ncs | | |
| `LONG` | string `string(null,BYTE)` lob, cs:db | | |
| `RAW(n)` | binary `binary(n)` | | |
| `LONG RAW` | binary `binary(null)` lob | | |
| `BLOB` | binary `binary(null)` lob | | |
| `BFILE` | NATIVE text `oracle.bfile.locator@1` | | The value is the locator. File content is never captured. |
| `BOOLEAN`, `BOOL` | boolean | | Oracle Database 23ai and later. |
| `DATE` | temporal `datetime/NONE/0`, years -4712..9999 | bce_years | Oracle DATE has a time component. Oracle uses the Julian calendar before 1582-10-15. The producer reads the stored calendar fields (year, month, day) and converts them to the proleptic Gregorian calendar of Section 6.3: fields before 1582-10-05 are Julian calendar fields, fields from 1582-10-15 are Gregorian and are unchanged. So 1 January 4712 BC (Julian) is `-4712-11-24`. Oracle can store the gap days 1582-10-05 to 1582-10-14; converted as Julian they would equal 1582-10-15 to 1582-10-24, so the conversion would not be one-to-one. The producer names a column holding a gap day in the unavailable-value report (Section 10). |
| `TIMESTAMP(p)`, `TIMESTAMP` (p = 6) | temporal `datetime/NONE/p`, years -4712..9999 | bce_years | p is 0 to 9. Calendar conversion as for `DATE`. |
| `TIMESTAMP(p) WITH TIME ZONE` | temporal `datetime/NAMED_ZONE_RETAINED/p`, years -4712..9999 | bce_years | Zone name written when stored. Calendar conversion as for `DATE`. |
| `TIMESTAMP(p) WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE` | temporal `datetime/SESSION_LOCAL/p`, years -4712..9999 | bce_years | The engine stores the value normalized to the database time zone; the producer writes the instant the engine returns for the value with `SESSIONTIMEZONE` set to `'+00:00'`, with `+00:00`; this fixes how a region `DBTIMEZONE` resolves an ambiguous wall time. Calendar conversion as for `DATE`. |
| `INTERVAL YEAR(y) TO MONTH` (y = 2) | interval `interval/YEAR_MONTH/CALENDAR/0`, `leading_precision` y | | |
| `INTERVAL DAY(d) TO SECOND(s)` (d = 2, s = 6) | interval `interval/DAY_TIME/ELAPSED/s`, `leading_precision` d | | |
| `JSON` | document `JSON`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` true | | Oracle Database 21c and later. Stored as OSON. Typed interface: the OSON value read through the typed JSON API (`OracleJsonParser` events or the `OracleJsonValue` object model). Ordinary number kind: the decimal scalar (`OracleJsonDecimal`, SQL `NUMBER`), with no trailing zeros in the coefficient. Other kinds map to tags as Section 6.2.11 lists. Date and timestamp scalars are converted to the proleptic Gregorian calendar as for `DATE`. `member_order_preserved` true: OSON keeps the written member order, and the producer writes it. |
| `XMLTYPE` stored as binary XML | document `XML`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | Canonical text: `XMLSERIALIZE(DOCUMENT col AS CLOB NO INDENT)` at Oracle 26ai; an engine-output codec (Section 5.3). Object-relational XMLType storage is unlisted. |
| `XMLTYPE` stored as CLOB | document `XML`, lexical_preserved true, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | |
| `VECTOR(n, FLOAT32)` | vector `dimension` n, `FLOAT32` | | |
| `VECTOR(n, FLOAT64)` | vector `dimension` n, `FLOAT64` | | |
| `VECTOR(n, INT8)` | vector `dimension` n, `INT8` | | |
| `VECTOR(n, BINARY)` | vector `dimension` n, `BINARY` | | n is a multiple of 8, so the byte length and `dimension` agree. |
| `VECTOR(n, t, SPARSE)` | vector `dimension` n, element per t, sparse | | Oracle Database 23.7 and later. |
| `VECTOR(*, t)` | vector `dimension` null, element per t | | |
| `VECTOR(n, *)`, `VECTOR(*, *)`, `VECTOR` | vector `dimension` n or null, `element_type` null | | Each value carries its format. |
| `SDO_GEOMETRY` | NATIVE text `oracle.sdo_geometry.sdo@1` | | The native structure is carried, because WKT cannot express Oracle's element encodings (optimized rectangles, circles, arcs, `SDO_POINT`, solids, LRS measures) and a WKT round trip stores different `SDO_ELEM_INFO` and `SDO_ORDINATES`. A consumer on another engine converts through `SDO_UTIL.TO_WKTGEOMETRY` semantics (Appendix A). |
| `ROWID` | identifier `ROWID`, stable false | | Characters: `ROWIDTOCHAR`, 18 characters. |
| `UROWID` | identifier `UROWID`, stable false | | A UROWID column can hold physical, logical or foreign rowids. Characters: `CAST(col AS VARCHAR2(4000))`. A physical rowid has 18 characters; a logical or foreign rowid has a variable length. |
| `ANYDATA` | NATIVE text `oracle.anydata.typed-json@1` | | |
| Object type `T`, column declared `NOT SUBSTITUTABLE` or `T` declared `FINAL` | struct `type_name` T, `fields` per the type's attributes | | Each attribute follows its own rule. |
| Object type `T`, substitutable column | NATIVE text `oracle.object.typed-json@1` | | The value carries its runtime type, which can be a subtype of T with more attributes. |
| `REF T` | NATIVE text `oracle.ref.hex@1` | | A reference, not a value. |
| `VARRAY(n) OF t` | array `element_type` per t, `max_cardinality` n, `rank` 1 | | |
| Nested table `TABLE OF t` | array `element_type` per t, `rank` 1 | | A nested table is unordered, and the engine's iteration order can change between reads. The producer sorts the elements in ascending order of the UTF-8 bytes of each element's base value form, with `null` spelled as `null`. The same set of elements is then always written the same way. |

Written against PostgreSQL 17. The rules cover that version and later versions (Section 7.1).

| Native type pattern | Family and traits | Flags | Attributes and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `boolean`, `bool` | boolean | | |
| `smallint`, `int2` | integer `integer/16/signed` | | `generated: "SEQUENCE"` when the column default is `nextval` of an owned sequence (`smallserial`); `"IDENTITY_ALWAYS"` when `attidentity` is `a`, `"IDENTITY_BY_DEFAULT"` when it is `d`; `"COMPUTED"` when `attgenerated` is set. `serial` never appears in `format_type` output. |
| `integer`, `int`, `int4` | integer `integer/32/signed` | | As above (`serial`). |
| `bigint`, `int8` | integer `integer/64/signed` | | As above (`bigserial`). |
| `oid`, `xid`, `cid` | integer `integer/32/unsigned` | | |
| `xid8` | integer `integer/64/unsigned` | | |
| `numeric(p,s)`, `decimal(p,s)` | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | nan | A declared precision rejects infinity ("numeric field overflow"); NaN is still stored. |
| `numeric(p)` | decimal `fixed(p,0)` | nan | As above. |
| `numeric`, `decimal` | decimal `variable(null)` | nan, infinity | |
| `real`, `float4` | decimal `binary(32)` | nan, infinity, signed_zero | |
| `double precision`, `float8` | decimal `binary(64)` | nan, infinity, signed_zero | |
| `money` | decimal `fixed(19,s)`, s the `frac_digits` of `lc_monetary` (2 in the default locale) | | The digits are the stored int64 scaled by `frac_digits` (`cash_numeric`), never the locale-formatted `cash_out` text. The producer MUST record `lc_monetary` in `attributes.locale`; a consumer sets the same `lc_monetary` before writing. |
| `character(n)`, `char(n)`, `bpchar(n)` | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)` fixed, cs:db | | |
| `character varying(n)`, `varchar(n)` | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)`, cs:db | | |
| `varchar`, `text`, `bpchar` | string `string(null,CODE_POINT)` lob, cs:db | | TOAST: an unchanged value may be absent from an update image. The same holds for every variable-length type; `lob` is set on the rows where it is usual. |
| `"char"` | binary `binary(1)` fixed | | The datum byte. `charout` prints byte 0x00 as the empty string, so the producer reads the byte, not the text. |
| `name` | string `string(63,BYTE)`, cs:db | | |
| `bytea` | binary `binary(null)` lob | | |
| `bit(n)` | bitstring `bit_length` n, fixed | | |
| `bit varying(n)`, `varbit(n)` | bitstring `bit_length` n | | |
| `bit varying`, `varbit` | bitstring `bit_length` null | | |
| `date` | temporal `date`, years -4713..5874897 | infinite_date, bce_years | The first representable day is 4714-11-24 BC (Julian day 0), which is `-4713-11-24` in the astronomical numbering of Section 6.3. |
| `time(p)`, `time` (p = 6) | temporal `time/NONE/p` | allows_24h | |
| `time(p) with time zone`, `timetz` | temporal `time/OFFSET_RETAINED/p` | allows_24h | The offset can carry seconds. |
| `timestamp(p)`, `timestamp` (p = 6) | temporal `datetime/NONE/p`, years -4713..294276 | infinite_date, bce_years | Range as for `date` at the low end. |
| `timestamp(p) with time zone`, `timestamptz` | temporal `datetime/UTC_INSTANT/p`, years -4713..294276 | infinite_date, bce_years | As above. |
| `interval`, `interval fields (p)` | interval `interval/MIXED/CALENDAR/p` (p = 6 when absent) | infinity | A fields qualifier narrows `interval_parts` only for `YEAR`, `MONTH` and `YEAR TO MONTH`, which give `YEAR_MONTH` with 0 fraction digits. Every other qualifier stays `MIXED`, because PostgreSQL clears only the fields below the qualifier: `'1 year 2 days'::interval day` keeps its months. |
| `uuid` | uuid | | `storage_byte_order: "RFC"` |
| `json` | document `JSON`, lexical_preserved true, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | |
| `jsonb` | document `JSON`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | Canonical text is `jsonb_out` (keys by length then bytes, `", "` and `": "` separators). |
| `xml` | document `XML`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | Canonical text: `xml_out` at PostgreSQL 17, an engine-output codec. The engine stores the input text, but every output path (`xml_out`, `xml_send`, the cast to `text`) drops a default XML declaration and rewrites a non-default one, so the stored text is not reachable through SQL; Section 10 declares the declaration loss. |

| `cidr` | network `CIDR` | | |
| `macaddr` | network `MAC`, octets 6 | | |

| composite type `T` | struct `type_name` T, `fields` per T | | |
| domain `D` over `t` | the rule for t | | |
| `hstore` | map, key `string(null,CODE_POINT)`, cs:db, `nullable` false; value `string(null,CODE_POINT)`, cs:db, `nullable` true | | Entries in UTF-8 byte order of the key (Section 6.5.2), not in `hstore_out` order. `map` has no `lob` trait; TOAST applies as for `text` (Section 10). |

| `geography` (PostGIS, unconstrained) | spatial `ANY`, `srid` null, dimension null, geodetic true, `ordinate_kind` BINARY64 | ordinate_specials | `srid_per_value: true` |

| `halfvec(n)` (pgvector) | vector `dimension` n, `FLOAT16` | | |
| `sparsevec(n)` (pgvector) | vector `dimension` n, `FLOAT32`, sparse | | |
| `vector`, `halfvec`, `sparsevec` (pgvector, no dimension) | as the rows above, `dimension` null | | |
| `point`, `line`, `lseg`, `box`, `path`, `polygon`, `circle` | NATIVE text `postgresql.geometric.text@1` | | Built-in geometric types; not OGC geometries. |
| `tsvector` | NATIVE text `postgresql.tsvector.text@1`; see 7.9 | | |
| `tsquery` | NATIVE text `postgresql.tsquery.text@1` | | |
| `pg_lsn` | NATIVE text `postgresql.pg_lsn.text@1` | | |
| `citext` | string `string(null,CODE_POINT)` lob, cs:db | | `attributes.collation` records the case-insensitive comparison: `"citext"`. |
| `ltree` | NATIVE text `postgresql.ltree.text@1` | | |
| `jsonpath` | NATIVE text `postgresql.jsonpath.text@1` | | |
| `tid` | NATIVE text `postgresql.tid.text@1` | | |
| user-defined range type over `t` (`CREATE TYPE ... AS RANGE`), where t maps to `integer`, `decimal` or `temporal` | range, element per t | infinity | The element descriptor keeps t's own flags (for example `nan`) under Section 4.18; the range's `infinity` flag replaces t's infinity flag. ## 7.6 MySQL

Written against MySQL 9.0. The rules cover that version and later versions (Section 7.1).

| Native type pattern | Family and traits | Flags | Attributes and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TINYINT`, `TINYINT(m)`, `BOOL`, `BOOLEAN` | integer `integer/8/signed` | | `display_width: m` when `COLUMN_TYPE` reports it (MySQL 9 reports it only for `TINYINT(1)` and `ZEROFILL` columns). `BOOL` is `TINYINT(1)`. Full range -128..127. Every integer row: `generated: "IDENTITY_BY_DEFAULT"` when `EXTRA` contains `auto_increment`; `"COMPUTED"` or `"VIRTUAL"` for a generated column. |
| `TINYINT UNSIGNED` | integer `integer/8/unsigned` | | |
| `SMALLINT` | integer `integer/16/signed` | | |
| `SMALLINT UNSIGNED` | integer `integer/16/unsigned` | | |
| `MEDIUMINT` | integer `integer/24/signed` | | |
| `MEDIUMINT UNSIGNED` | integer `integer/24/unsigned` | | |
| `INT`, `INTEGER` | integer `integer/32/signed` | | |
| `INT UNSIGNED` | integer `integer/32/unsigned` | | |
| `BIGINT` | integer `integer/64/signed` | | |
| `BIGINT UNSIGNED` | integer `integer/64/unsigned` | | `SERIAL` resolves to this pattern with `auto_increment`, so `generated: "IDENTITY_BY_DEFAULT"`. |
| `YEAR` | integer `integer/16/unsigned`, max "2155" | | Zero is the zero value. Years 1901 to 2155 otherwise. |
| `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `NUMERIC(p,s)`, `DEC(p,s)`, `FIXED(p,s)` | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | | p ≤ 65, s ≤ 30. `DECIMAL` alone is `(10,0)`; `DECIMAL(p)` is `(p,0)`. |
| `FLOAT`, `FLOAT(p)` with p ≤ 24; also with `UNSIGNED`, `ZEROFILL` or `(M,D)` | decimal `binary(32)` | signed_zero | MySQL stores no NaN or infinity. It keeps the sign of zero. `UNSIGNED`, `ZEROFILL` and `(M,D)` narrow or format the value and do not change the rule. |
| `FLOAT(p)` with p > 24, `DOUBLE`, `DOUBLE PRECISION`; also with `UNSIGNED`, `ZEROFILL` or `(M,D)` | decimal `binary(64)` | signed_zero | As above. |
| `BIT(n)`, `BIT` (n = 1) | bitstring `bit_length` n, fixed | | |
| `CHAR(n)` | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)`, cs:col | | Not `fixed`: the engine removes trailing spaces on retrieval, so padding is not part of the value. |
| `VARCHAR(n)` | string `string(n,CODE_POINT)`, cs:col | | |
| `TINYTEXT` | string `string(255,BYTE)` lob, cs:col | | The limit is in bytes, whatever the character set. |
| `TEXT` | string `string(65535,BYTE)` lob, cs:col | | As above. |
| `MEDIUMTEXT` | string `string(16777215,BYTE)` lob, cs:col | | As above. |
| `LONGTEXT` | string `string(4294967295,BYTE)` lob, cs:col | | As above. |
| `BINARY(n)` | binary `binary(n)` fixed | | Zero-padded to n. |
| `VARBINARY(n)` | binary `binary(n)` | | |
| `TINYBLOB`, `BLOB`, `MEDIUMBLOB`, `LONGBLOB` | binary `binary(n)` lob, n 255, 65535, 16777215 or 4294967295 | | |
| `DATE` | temporal `date`, years 0..9999 | bce_years, zero_date, incomplete_date, nonexistent_date | The documented range starts at 1000, but the engine stores years 0 to 999. `bce_years` is set because year 0000 is below 0001 (Section 4.8); no year below 0000 is stored. |
| `TIME(fsp)`, `TIME` (fsp = 0) | interval `interval/DAY_TIME/ELAPSED/fsp` | | Range -838:59:59 to 838:59:59. |
| `DATETIME(fsp)`, `DATETIME` (fsp = 0) | temporal `datetime/NONE/fsp`, years 0..9999 | bce_years, zero_date, incomplete_date, nonexistent_date | As for `DATE`. |
| `TIMESTAMP(fsp)`, `TIMESTAMP` (fsp = 0) | temporal `datetime/UTC_INSTANT/fsp`, years 1970..2038 | zero_date | `auto_update: true` when `ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` is declared. |
| `ENUM('a','b',…)` | enumeration `allowed_values` in declaration order, ordered true, multi_select false, by_index false | error_value | Labels are read from `COLUMN_TYPE`: each label is a single-quoted string in which `''` is one quote and `\\` is one backslash; the engine stores labels with trailing spaces removed. `attributes.collation` is set. |
| `SET('a','b',…)` | enumeration `allowed_values` in declaration order, ordered false, multi_select true, by_index false | | |
| `ENUM(…)` with a duplicate label under the column collation (permitted outside strict mode; `ENUM('a','A')` in a `_ci` collation is such a case). Exception to the `ENUM` row. | enumeration `allowed_values` in declaration order, ordered true, multi_select false, by_index true | error_value | Values travel as one-based member indexes. |
| `SET(…)` with a duplicate label under the column collation (permitted outside strict mode). Exception to the `SET` row. | enumeration `allowed_values` in declaration order, ordered false, multi_select true, by_index true | | Values travel as ascending one-based member indexes, read from the stored bitmask: bit i, counted from 0, gives member i + 1. Mask 5 is `[1,3]`. |
| `JSON` | document `JSON`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` true | | Typed interface: the binary JSON value with the kinds `JSON_TYPE` reports. Ordinary number kinds: `INTEGER` and `UNSIGNED INTEGER`, written as plain digits (`100`, never `1E+2`, which the engine would re-parse as `DOUBLE`); the coefficient rule of Section 6.2.3 does not apply to them. Other kinds map to tags as Section 6.2.11 lists. `member_order_preserved` false: the engine stores members sorted by key length then bytes, and the producer writes that order. |
| `GEOMETRY` | spatial `ANY`, `srid` per column (null when none), dimension 2, `ordinate_kind` BINARY64 | | Ordinates from `ST_AsBinary`. `srid_per_value: true` when the column has no SRID attribute. `geodetic` is true when the column's SRID is geographic, false when it is projected or 0, and null when the SRID is per value. Ordinates longitude first (`ST_AsText` with `axis-order=long-lat`). |
| `POINT`, `LINESTRING`, `POLYGON`, `MULTIPOINT`, `MULTILINESTRING`, `MULTIPOLYGON`, `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION` | spatial `geometry_kind` as named, `srid` and `geodetic` as for `GEOMETRY`, dimension 2, `ordinate_kind` BINARY64 | | |
| `VECTOR(n)` | vector `dimension` null, `FLOAT32` | | MySQL `VECTOR(n)` is a maximum element count, not an exact dimension, so `dimension` is null; `max_length` of the declaration is not a trait. |
