| Native type pattern | Family and traits | Flags | Attributes and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BOOLEAN` | boolean | | |
| `SMALLINT` | integer `integer/16/signed` | | |
| `INTEGER`, `INT` | integer `integer/32/signed` | | |
| `BIGINT` | integer `integer/64/signed` | | |
| `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `NUMERIC(p,s)`, `DEC(p,s)`, `NUM(p,s)` | decimal `fixed(p,s)` | | p ≤ 31. `DECIMAL` alone is `(5,0)`. |
| `DECFLOAT(16)` | decimal `decfloat(16)` | nan, signaling_nan, infinity, signed_zero | The sign of NaN and sNaN is kept (`"-NaN"`, `"-sNaN"`). |
| `DECFLOAT(34)`, `DECFLOAT` | decimal `decfloat(34)` | nan, signaling_nan, infinity, signed_zero | As above. |
| `REAL` | decimal `binary(32)` | signed_zero | Db2 stores no NaN or infinity. It keeps the sign of zero. |
| `DOUBLE`, `DOUBLE PRECISION`, `FLOAT`, `FLOAT(n)` with n > 24 | decimal `binary(64)` | signed_zero | `FLOAT(n)` with n ≤ 24 is `REAL`. As above. |
| `CHAR(n)`, `CHARACTER(n)` | string `string(n,BYTE)` fixed, cs:db | | Under `CODEUNITS32` string units, `length_unit` is `CODE_POINT` and `length_semantics_source` is `CODEUNITS32`. |
| `VARCHAR(n)`, `CHARACTER VARYING(n)` | string `string(n,BYTE)`, cs:db | | As above for string units. |
| `CLOB(n)` | string `string(n,BYTE)` lob, cs:db | | As `VARCHAR` for string units. |
| `GRAPHIC(n)` | string `string(n,UTF16_UNIT)` fixed, charset UTF-16 | | In a Unicode database. Under `CODEUNITS32` string units, `length_unit` is `CODE_POINT`. In a non-Unicode DBCS database the graphic data is in that code page and Section 7.10 applies. |
| `VARGRAPHIC(n)` | string `string(n,UTF16_UNIT)`, charset UTF-16 | | |
| `DBCLOB(n)` | string `string(n,UTF16_UNIT)` lob, charset UTF-16 | | |
| `LONG VARCHAR` | string `string(32700,BYTE)` lob, cs:db | | Deprecated, still reported by the catalog. |
| `LONG VARCHAR FOR BIT DATA` | binary `binary(32700)` lob | | |
| `LONG VARGRAPHIC` | string `string(16350,UTF16_UNIT)` lob, charset UTF-16 | | |
| structured type `T` (`CREATE TYPE ... AS ... MODE DB2SQL`) | NATIVE text `db2.structured.typed-json@1` | | A structured-type column is substitutable: the value carries its dynamic type, which can be a subtype of T with more attributes. `attributes.type_schema` records `TYPESCHEMA`. |
| `REF(T)` | NATIVE text `db2.ref.hex@1` | | A reference, not a value. |
| distinct type `D` over `t` | the rule for t | | `source_type` is `D`; `attributes.type_schema` records `TYPESCHEMA`. The consumer recreates `D` from the catalog, not from the descriptor. |
| `DB2SECURITYLABEL` | binary `binary(128)` | | Policy-bound bytes; meaningful only under the same security policy. |
| `NCHAR(n)`, `NVARCHAR(n)`, `NCLOB(n)` | as `GRAPHIC`, `VARGRAPHIC`, `DBCLOB`; under `nchar_mapping` `CHAR_CU32`, as `CHAR(n CODEUNITS32)`, `VARCHAR(n CODEUNITS32)`, `CLOB(n CODEUNITS32)` | | Synonyms in a Unicode database. The catalog reports the resolved type, which this row names. |
| `CHAR(n) FOR BIT DATA`, `CHARACTER(n) FOR BIT DATA` | binary `binary(n)` fixed | | |
| `VARCHAR(n) FOR BIT DATA` | binary `binary(n)` | | |
| `BINARY(n)` | binary `binary(n)` fixed | | |
| `VARBINARY(n)` | binary `binary(n)` | | |
| `BLOB(n)` | binary `binary(n)` lob | | |
| `DATE` | temporal `date`, years 1..9999 | | |
| `TIME` | temporal `time/NONE/0` | allows_24h | |
| `TIMESTAMP(p)`, `TIMESTAMP` (p = 6) | temporal `datetime/NONE/p`, years 1..9999 | allows_24h | p is 0 to 12. |
| `XML` | document `XML`, lexical_preserved false, lob, `scalar_extensions` false | | Canonical text: `XMLSERIALIZE(col AS CLOB(2G) INCLUDING XMLDECLARATION)` at Db2 12.1, an engine-output codec. |
| `ST_GEOMETRY` and subtypes | spatial `ANY` or the subtype's kind (`ANY` for the abstract subtypes `ST_CURVE`, `ST_SURFACE`, `ST_MULTICURVE`, `ST_MULTISURFACE`), `srid` null, dimension null, geodetic false, `ordinate_kind` BINARY64 | | `srid_per_value: true`. Ordinates from the stored doubles through an interface that keeps Z and M (`ST_AsBinary` where it emits Z and M on the Db2 release; to be confirmed by the Db2 owner), not from `ST_AsText`, which rounds. |

## 7.9 NATIVE codecs

This section defines each codec that the dictionary names. A codec is a grammar with an inverse. Six codecs are engine-output codecs (Section 5.3): `postgresql.tsvector.text@1`, `postgresql.tsquery.text@1`, `postgresql.geometric.text@1`, `postgresql.ltree.text@1`, `postgresql.jsonpath.text@1` and `sqlserver.clr_udt.bytes@1`. The first five are pinned to PostgreSQL 17 output, and their test vectors are that output. The canonical XML text that each engine's `document` row names is an engine-output codec in the same sense, pinned to the function and version the row states. `sqlserver.clr_udt.bytes@1` is pinned to the type's own `Write` method. Its inverse needs the user's assembly, so its `vectors` field holds the bytes of a registered sample type, not a portable corpus. The text of a `text` carrier is the string that the grammar produces. The bytes of a `binary` carrier are the bytes that the grammar produces.

| Codec | Carrier | Grammar | Inverse |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sqlserver.hierarchyid.path@1` | text | The canonical path string: `/`, then for each level the level's integer labels separated by `.`, each level ended by `/`. Labels are decimal integers without leading zeros; negative labels carry a minus sign. The root is `/`. This is the output of `ToString()`. | `hierarchyid::Parse`. |
| `sqlserver.sql_variant.typed-json@1` | text | A JSON text with exactly three members in order: `base_type`, the base type exactly as the Section 3.2 template writes a column of that type from `SQL_VARIANT_PROPERTY` (`BaseType`, `Precision`, `Scale`, `MaxLength`): `DECIMAL(10,2)`, `NVARCHAR(50)` (`MaxLength` 100 bytes halved), `FLOAT(53)`, `DATETIME2(7)`, with the parameters always written; `collation`, the collation name for character base types and `null` otherwise; and `value`, the value in the JSON binding form of the family the dictionary assigns to that base type under that collation. No whitespace. | Read `base_type` and `collation`, resolve the rule, decode `value`. |
| `sqlserver.clr_udt.bytes@1` | binary | The bytes returned by the type's `Write` method, as the engine stores them. | The type's `Read` method. |
| `postgresql.tsvector.text@1` | text | The output of `tsvector_out` in PostgreSQL 17: every lexeme single-quoted, with internal quotes and backslashes doubled, each followed by `:` and its positions with weights when the lexeme has positions, and by nothing when it has none, lexemes separated by one space, sorted by lexeme. | `tsvector_in`. |
| `postgresql.tsquery.text@1` | text | The output of `tsquery_out` in PostgreSQL 17. | `tsquery_in`. |
| `postgresql.geometric.text@1` | text | The output of the type's `_out` function in PostgreSQL 17 for `point`, `line`, `lseg`, `box`, `path`, `polygon` and `circle`, with `extra_float_digits` at its default of 1, which prints shortest round-trip digits. | The type's `_in` function. |
| `postgresql.pg_lsn.text@1` | text | Two upper-case hexadecimal numbers separated by `/`, without leading zeros. | `pg_lsn_in`. |
| `postgresql.ltree.text@1` | text | The output of `ltree_out` in PostgreSQL 17, an engine-output codec: labels separated by `.`; a label has 1 to 1000 characters, which are the database locale's alphanumerics, `_` and `-`; the empty path is the empty string. | `ltree_in`. |
| `postgresql.jsonpath.text@1` | text | The output of `jsonpath_out` in PostgreSQL 17, an engine-output codec; the engine normalizes the path (`$.a` becomes `$."a"`). | `jsonpath_in`. |
| `postgresql.tid.text@1` | text | `"(" uint "," uint ")"`: block number and offset. | `tidin`. |
| `db2.structured.typed-json@1` | text | As `oracle.object.typed-json@1`, with `type` the schema-qualified dynamic type of the value (`TYPE_NAME`, `TYPE_SCHEMA`). | Construct the dynamic type. |
| `db2.ref.hex@1` | text | The reference's `FOR BIT DATA` representation in upper-case hexadecimal, the `ref-hex` production of `oracle.ref.hex@1`. | Cast from the bytes to `REF(T)`. |
| `oracle.bfile.locator@1` | text | A JSON text with exactly two members in order: `directory`, the directory object name exactly as stored; and `filename`, the file name. No whitespace. | `BFILENAME(directory, filename)`. |
| `oracle.object.typed-json@1` | text | A JSON text with exactly three members in order: `type`, the runtime object type name as `SYS_TYPEID` resolves it, schema-qualified; `descriptor`, a `struct` descriptor for that runtime type, with `nullable`, as Section 4.1 defines nested descriptors; and `value`, the value in the `struct` form of that descriptor. No whitespace. | Read `descriptor`, decode `value`, construct the runtime type. |
| `oracle.ref.hex@1` | text | The output of `REFTOHEX`: an even number of upper-case hexadecimal digits, `ref-hex = 2*( 2( DIGIT / %x41-46 ) )`. | `HEXTOREF`. |
| `oracle.sdo_geometry.sdo@1` | text | A JSON text with exactly five members in order: `gtype`, the `SDO_GTYPE` as a JSON number; `srid`, the `SDO_SRID` as a JSON number or `null`; `point`, `null` or an array of three elements (`x`, `y`, `z`), each the finite scientific string of Section 6.2.3 or `null`; `elem_info`, an array of JSON numbers (`SDO_ELEM_INFO`) or `null`; `ordinates`, an array of the finite scientific strings of Section 6.2.3 (`SDO_ORDINATES`) or `null`. No whitespace. Numbers in `ordinates` and `point` keep Oracle's no-scale coefficient rule. | Construct `SDO_GEOMETRY(gtype, srid, point, elem_info, ordinates)`. |
| `oracle.anydata.typed-json@1` | text | A JSON text with exactly three members in order: `type`, the Oracle type name as `ANYDATA.GETTYPENAME` returns it; `descriptor`, a nested descriptor (`logical_type`, `parameters`, `nullable` false) built from the type's full declaration as `ANYDATA.GETTYPE` reports it, so that the deciding traits are present; and `value`, the value in the JSON binding form of that descriptor, or `null` for a typed null (`ANYDATA.CONVERTNUMBER(NULL)`). No whitespace. | Read `descriptor`, decode `value`. |

## 7.10 Character sets carried as bytes

Each character set in this table has no one-to-one conversion to Unicode. Either it has more than one code point for at least one Unicode character, or the engine defines no conversion at all. A column in one of these character sets is `binary` with the `charset` trait (Section 6.11). A character set not in this table is carried as `string`.

| Engine | Character set | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| mysql | `cp932`, `sjis`, `eucjpms`, `ujis` | NEC and IBM extension rows duplicate JIS X 0208 characters; `sjis` also maps both 0x5C and 0x815F to U+005C. |
| mysql | `big5` | Duplicate encodings of several characters. |
| oracle | `JA16SJIS`, `JA16SJISTILDE`, `JA16EUC`, `JA16EUCTILDE` | As `cp932`. |
| oracle | `ZHT16BIG5`, `ZHT16MSWIN950`, `ZHT16HKSCS` | As `big5`. |
| sqlserver | `cp932` (collations on code page 932, `Japanese_*` non-Unicode) | As mysql `cp932`, for `CHAR`, `VARCHAR` and `TEXT`. |
| sqlserver | `cp950` (collations on code page 950, `Chinese_Taiwan_*` non-Unicode) | As `big5`: 0xA2CC and 0xA451 both map to U+5341. |
| db2 | `IBM-943`, `IBM-941` | As `cp932`. `IBM-941` is the pure-DBCS code page of `GRAPHIC` data in an `IBM-943` database. |
| db2 | `IBM-950`, `big5` | As `big5`. |
| postgresql | `SQL_ASCII`, `MULE_INTERNAL` | The engine defines no conversion to Unicode, so the bytes are the only faithful value. |
| postgresql | `EUC_JP` | As `cp932`: NEC-selected and IBM extension rows duplicate characters. |

A character set wrongly listed here still round-trips, because bytes carry everything. A character set wrongly omitted loses data silently. The table therefore lists every character set known to have a duplicate encoding; an engine owner removes a row only with evidence that the conversion is one-to-one.

## 7.11 Patterns without a rule of their own

| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| On a covered engine, a user-defined type built on another type (PostgreSQL domain, Db2 distinct type, SQL Server alias type, Oracle 23ai SQL domain) | The rule for the base type. `source_type` keeps the user-defined name and `attributes.type_schema` its schema, so a consumer can recreate it from the catalog. An Oracle object subtype is not this case: Section 7.4 maps it as an object type of its own. |
| On a covered engine, a composite or object type, unless a more specific rule applies (Oracle substitutable objects, Section 7.4) | `struct`, each field by its own rule. |
| On a covered engine, a collection type | `array`, the element by its own rule. |
| A type with no rule, such as an extension type | Unlisted. The producer chooses a family or NATIVE and sets `listed: false` (P-TYPE-10). |
| An engine the dictionary does not cover | Every type is unlisted. The producer chooses a family or NATIVE for each type and sets `listed: false` (P-TYPE-10). |

A producer that chooses a family for an unlisted type writes a full descriptor for that family. Every applicable trait is stated, and every value is in the base value form. A consumer reads such a column as it reads any column of that family. `listed: false` tells the consumer that the mapping is the producer's own: another producer on the same source can choose a different family or different traits. Those streams are not interoperable for that column until the dictionary gains a rule. The producer SHOULD publish the mapping it chose.

## 7.12 Managed services, builds and compatible engines

Most deployments of the covered engines run as a cloud service or as a vendor build. This section says when such a deployment is the engine, so that its producer uses the engine's token and the engine's dictionary table, and when it is not.

**A managed service or build is the engine** when all three hold:

1. It runs the engine's own code, with or without vendor patches, and the engine's catalog reports the engine's own version string (`version()`, `@@version`, `V$VERSION`, `SYSIBMADM.ENV_INST_INFO`).
2. Every type that the engine's dictionary table lists keeps the engine's storage and value domain. A service that limits what a user can create does not fail this test; a service that changes how a listed type stores or orders values does.
3. The change images that the producer reads come from the engine's own log or replication interface, even if the service wraps it. Those interfaces are logical decoding, the binlog, LogMiner, the transaction log and the Db2 log.

Then the producer uses the engine's token and the engine version the catalog reports, and the applicable rule set is the engine's. A type the service adds is unlisted under P-TYPE-10. Aurora PostgreSQL adds none; AlloyDB's `alloydb_scann` types are index types, not column types. The producer records the service in STREAM_METADATA (Specification Section 10.4, `source_engine_variant`), because a consumer or an operator may need it, but no dictionary rule depends on it.

| Engine token | Managed services and builds that are the engine (as of November 2026) |
|---|---|
| `postgresql` | Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Google Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Google AlloyDB, Supabase, Neon, Crunchy Bridge, EDB Postgres Advanced Server in PostgreSQL mode, Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL, Oracle Database with PostgreSQL (OCI Database with PostgreSQL) |
| `mysql` | Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon Aurora MySQL, Azure Database for MySQL, Google Cloud SQL for MySQL, Oracle MySQL HeatWave, Percona Server for MySQL |
| `mariadb` | Amazon RDS for MariaDB, Azure Database for MariaDB, SkySQL |
| `sqlserver` | Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Google Cloud SQL for SQL Server |
| `oracle` | Oracle Autonomous Database, Oracle Exadata Database Service, Oracle Base Database Service, Oracle Database@Azure, @Google Cloud and @AWS, Amazon RDS for Oracle |
| `db2` | IBM Db2 on Cloud, IBM Db2 Warehouse, Amazon RDS for Db2 |

A service in this table can fail test 3 for a particular capture path. Azure SQL Database exposes change tracking and CDC tables but not the transaction log. A producer that reads CDC tables still reads the engine's own change images, so it is the engine. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL exposes logical decoding; a producer that reads Aurora's own activity-stream format is reading the engine's images in another container and is the engine.

**A compatible engine is not the engine.** It has its own token. Every type is unlisted until the dictionary gains a table for it, even when the product calls its types by the engine's names. The reason is fidelity. A compatible engine's `DECIMAL`, `INTERVAL`, `TIMESTAMP` or `JSON` can have a different value domain, storage or canonical text, and the dictionary rule would then be wrong on the wire. A producer on such an engine applies P-TYPE-10, and SHOULD start from the nearest engine's table when it chooses its mappings.

| Not the engine | Nearest table | Known type differences (examples, not a dictionary) |
|---|---|---|
| CockroachDB | 7.5 | `DECIMAL` admits NaN and Infinity under its own rules; `INTERVAL` has no field qualifiers; no `xid`, `oid` semantics; `JSONB` only |
| YugabyteDB | 7.5 | PostgreSQL code at a pinned major version, but its own storage; treated as compatible until an owner confirms test 2 |
| Amazon Aurora DSQL | 7.5 | PostgreSQL-compatible interface, different engine; no `jsonb`, limited types |
| Google Spanner, PostgreSQL interface | 7.5 | Spanner types under PostgreSQL names; `NUMERIC` is Spanner `NUMERIC` (38, 9); no `interval` |
| TiDB | 7.6 | MySQL-compatible; its own `DECIMAL`, `JSON` and `TIMESTAMP` implementations |
| OceanBase (MySQL and Oracle modes), PolarDB, GaussDB / openGauss | 7.6, 7.4, 7.5 | Compatibility modes over a different engine |
| Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL | 7.7 | SQL Server interface over PostgreSQL storage; the engine is `postgresql`, and the T-SQL types are views over PostgreSQL types |
| SingleStore, Vitess, PlanetScale, ProxySQL | 7.6 | Vitess and ProxySQL front MySQL and are the engine when the backing database is MySQL; SingleStore is its own engine |
| EDB Postgres Advanced Server in Oracle-compatible mode | 7.5 | Oracle-named types (`NUMBER`, `VARCHAR2`, `DATE` with time) over PostgreSQL storage; the engine is `postgresql`, and the catalog reports the PostgreSQL types |

An owner can move a product from the second table to the first by confirming the three tests, which is a dictionary change, not a model change.

## 7.13 MariaDB

Written against MariaDB 11.8 (long-term support). The rules cover that version and later versions (Section 7.1).

MariaDB forked from MySQL in 2009 and has its own catalog, type set and binary log. It is its own engine, with the token `mariadb`. Every rule of the MySQL table (Section 7.6) applies to MariaDB unchanged, except as the table below says. A pattern not in this table matches the MySQL rule. The settings of Section 7.1 apply (character set, collation per column). The `source_type` template is `information_schema.COLUMNS.COLUMN_TYPE`, as for MySQL.

| Native type pattern | Family and traits | Flags | Attributes and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `JSON` | string `string(4294967295,BYTE)` lob, cs:col | | MariaDB `JSON` is an alias of `LONGTEXT` with a `JSON_VALID` check; the engine stores the text as written and has no binary JSON kinds. It is not `document`, because no canonical form or typed interface exists; a consumer that wants `document` semantics treats the text as the document. `attributes.collation` is set. |
| `UUID` | uuid | | MariaDB 10.7 and later. Stored in a byte order that sorts by the time fields; the wire spelling is the RFC form. `storage_byte_order: "MIXED"` |
| `INET4` | network `INET` | | MariaDB 10.10 and later. A host address only, so the prefix is always `/32`. |
| `INET6` | network `INET`, octets null | | MariaDB 10.5 and later. A host address only, so the prefix is always `/128`. An IPv4-mapped address is stored as IPv6 and written as `::ffff:c000:201/128`. |
| `VECTOR(n)` | vector `dimension` n, `FLOAT32` | | MariaDB 11.7 and later. `n` is the exact dimension. |
| `GEOMETRY` and the seven subtypes | as MySQL, with `srid` null and `geodetic` false | | MariaDB stores an SRID per value but computes on a flat plane for every SRID; `srid_per_value: true`. Ordinates from `ST_AsBinary`. |
| `BOOLEAN` | integer `integer/8/signed` | | As MySQL `TINYINT(1)`. |
| `DATETIME(fsp)`, `TIMESTAMP(fsp)`, `TIME(fsp)` | as MySQL | | `fsp` 0 to 6. MariaDB `TIMESTAMP` covers 1970 to 2106 on 64-bit builds from 11.5; the row sets `year_max` 2106 on those builds and 2038 otherwise, which the producer reads from `@@version` and the platform. |
| `ENUM`, `SET` | as MySQL | error_value (ENUM) | Duplicate-label detection under the column collation, as MySQL. |
| Any type, column with `GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START` or `ROW END` (system-versioned tables) | the base type's rule | | `auto_update: true`; the consumer does not write them (C-TYPE-11). |
| Any type, `DEFAULT NEXTVAL(seq)` | the base type's rule | | `generated: "SEQUENCE"`. |
| Any type under `sql_mode=ORACLE` | the rule for the resolved MariaDB type | | Oracle-named declarations (`VARCHAR2`, `NUMBER`, `DATE`) resolve in the catalog to MariaDB types; `COLUMN_TYPE` reports the resolved type, so the Oracle names never match. |
| `INT1` to `INT8`, `MIDDLEINT`, `FLOAT4`, `FLOAT8`, `LONG`, `LONG VARCHAR` | the rule for the resolved MariaDB type | | Aliases; the catalog reports the resolved type. |
# 8. Other Bindings

The family, the traits and the value domain do not depend on the serialization. Only the spelling does. A binding is the document that gives each valid combination of each family, and each NATIVE carrier, one representation in one serialization, with an inverse. Section 6 is the JSON binding. A binding for Avro, Protocol Buffers, Arrow or another serialization is a separate document.

A binding that conforms to this document:

1. Gives one representation for each valid trait combination of each family, and for each NATIVE carrier.
2. Holds the full declared domain of each combination. If the serialization's own type cannot, the binding carries the text form of Section 6 for that combination as a string, and says so. The binding uses a serialization's native type only where that type converts to and from the base value form without loss.
3. Gives an inverse decoder and test vectors for each representation, as Section 6 does.
4. Leaves the dictionary alone. A dictionary rule names a family and traits, never a serialization.
5. Publishes its type-encoding table. The table has one row per valid combination and per NATIVE carrier. Each row gives the serialization type, how the binding carries the descriptor (traits and flags) and nullability, and any conversion.

These are properties of a binding document. The producer rule that enforces them is P-TYPE-8. A producer that uses a serialization with no published binding MUST publish its own type-encoding table with these properties (P-TYPE-8). Until a binding exists, interoperability with other producers in that serialization is undefined.

Two patterns recur. A binary serialization often holds a value natively, so the digit-string and Base64 work of JSON disappears: `integer/64/unsigned` is an Arrow `UInt64`. If the serialization has a gap, such as decimal floating point or negative scale, the binding reuses the text grammar. It does not invent a new one. `decimal/decfloat/34` is an Arrow `Utf8` that holds the scientific string of Section 6.2.3. That is why Section 6 defines grammars for the text forms, not only for JSON.

# 9. Requirements

These rules bind the producer. `requirements.yaml` registers them, and the requirements register of the Specification summarizes them.

- P-TYPE-1: Producers MUST populate `source_type` with the column's type declaration as the engine's catalog reports it. Where the catalog reports it in parts, the producer assembles it by the template of Section 3.2. Normalization, aliasing, or expansion of what the catalog reports is non-conformant.

- P-TYPE-2: For a listed type, producers MUST populate `logical_type` and `parameters` as the matching rule in the applicable rule set assigns. The rule matches by the column's engine, engine version and native type pattern. For a family, that is every applicable domain trait and every capability flag that is true. A domain trait that does not apply to the family and its deciding traits MUST be absent. For NATIVE, that is the parameters of Section 5. The mapping MUST be deterministic. The same native type pattern, from the same engine and version, under the same database and column settings that the rule names, always produces the same descriptor. Section 7.1 lists those settings. A producer MUST NOT emit a column under a family if it does not know the value of an applicable domain trait of that family.

- P-TYPE-3: Producers MUST write each DML column value in the base value form that the column's family and deciding traits select in the binding in use. Producers MUST follow the grammar of that form exactly. The same source value MUST always produce the same characters.

- P-TYPE-4: Producers MUST NOT silently truncate, round, replace, or reduce the precision of any value. Producers MUST NOT convert a special value to null or to an ordinary value. If a producer cannot capture or write a value at full source fidelity, it MUST name the column in the unavailable-value report for that image. It MUST NOT silently alter the value.

- P-TYPE-5: If a rule in the applicable rule set assigns a family to a native type, producers MUST NOT emit the column as NATIVE.

- P-TYPE-6: If a rule in the applicable rule set assigns NATIVE to a native type, producers MUST use the carrier and the codec that the rule names.

- P-TYPE-7: This rule applies to an unlisted type that a producer emits as NATIVE. The producer MUST set `listed` to `false`. It MUST name a carrier and a codec. It SHOULD publish the grammar and the inverse of the codec where consumers of the stream can obtain them. No interoperability with other producers is claimed for such a column.

- P-TYPE-8: A producer that uses a serialization other than JSON MUST follow a binding that meets Section 8, or MUST publish its own type-encoding table that does. The producer MUST use a serialization's native type only where that type converts to and from the base value form without loss. Otherwise it MUST carry the base value form as a string.

- P-TYPE-9: Producers MUST NOT emit a special value (Section 6.8) for a column unless the descriptor of the column declares the capability flag that admits it as `true`. Producers MUST write each special value in its one spelling.

- P-TYPE-10: For an unlisted type, a producer MAY emit the column under a family or as NATIVE. Under a family, the descriptor MUST state every applicable domain trait of that family, and every value MUST be in the base value form; P-TYPE-3, P-TYPE-4 and P-TYPE-9 apply. Under NATIVE, P-TYPE-7 applies. In both cases the producer MUST set `listed` to `false`. The producer SHOULD publish the mapping it chose. No interoperability with other producers is claimed for such a column.

# 10. Known Limitations (Informative)

This section lists what this document does not yet cover, or covers in a way that has a known cost. Each entry states the limitation and its consequence.

- **Unpaired surrogates.** A value that contains an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate has no spelling (Section 6.9.2 rule 5) and is a decode failure. An engine that stores UTF-16 code units can hold such a value (SQL Server `NVARCHAR`, Oracle `AL16UTF16` and `CLOB`, MySQL `ucs2`, Db2 `GRAPHIC`). A producer on such an engine names those columns in the unavailable-value report and writes `null` in place of the value.

- **Values absent from change images.** The `lob` trait marks the columns for which `_lob_overflow` is usual. On PostgreSQL, TOAST can withhold an unchanged value of any variable-length type from an update image, not only of the columns the dictionary marks. A consumer on PostgreSQL may therefore see `_lob_overflow` name a column whose descriptor has `lob: false` or no `lob` trait at all. Oracle extended `VARCHAR2`, `NVARCHAR2` and `RAW` (above 4000 bytes under `MAX_STRING_SIZE=EXTENDED`) are stored as LOBs and can be withheld the same way.

- **Documents, enumeration labels and NATIVE text in a byte-carried character set.** These forms are strings. A value in a character set that Section 7.10 carries as bytes has no byte-carried spelling in them, so the producer names the column in the unavailable-value report (P-TYPE-4). This affects, for example, a `json` column in a PostgreSQL `SQL_ASCII` database and an `ENUM` column in MySQL `cp932`.

- **Mappings of unlisted types.** A producer on an engine or type that the dictionary does not cover chooses its own mapping (P-TYPE-10). Two producers on the same source can choose differently, and publication of the choice is recommended, not required. Their streams are not interoperable for those columns until the dictionary gains rules for that engine or type.

- **Large integers inside tagged documents.** In the tagged form, a MySQL `INTEGER` or `UNSIGNED INTEGER` scalar, and an Oracle `NUMBER` scalar, is an unquoted JSON number, even above 2^53. The document string is exact, but a consumer that parses it with a binary64-based JSON parser loses precision. Column values of the `integer` family do not have this problem, because `integer/64` is a digit string.

- **Document kinds the engine folds.** The tagged form keeps the kinds the engine's typed interface distinguishes. MySQL reports `DATETIME` and `TIMESTAMP` scalars, and `INTEGER` and `UNSIGNED INTEGER` scalars, through the same interface kinds, so `JSON_TYPE` on the restored document can differ from the source for those pairs; the values are equal. The precision of a MySQL JSON `DECIMAL` node is not carried, so `JSON_STORAGE_SIZE` can differ after a round trip. OSON's compact integer encodings are folded into one number spelling. A MySQL JSON temporal scalar that holds a zero or incomplete date has no spelling, because a `document` column carries no temporal flags; the producer names the column in the unavailable-value report.

- **Oracle dates in the 1582 calendar gap.** Oracle can store the dates 1582-10-05 to 1582-10-14, which do not exist in the proleptic Gregorian calendar of Section 6.3 once earlier dates are read as Julian. Each would collide with a real date ten days later, so the producer names such a column in the unavailable-value report instead of writing a value (Section 7.4).

- **Spatial values Well-Known Text cannot hold.** A SQL Server geometry whose points carry Z or M on some points and not others, a SQL Server `FULLGLOBE`, and an Oracle `SDO_GEOMETRY` mapped by a consumer to WKT (solids, arcs, optimized rectangles, LRS measures) are the known cases. The Oracle column is NATIVE so that a same-engine exchange keeps them; the SQL Server cases go to the unavailable-value report.

- **XML declaration on PostgreSQL.** `xml_out` drops a default XML declaration and rewrites a non-default one, so the stored declaration is not carried; the document content is.

- **Negative zero in exact decimals and NaN bit patterns.** A NaN in a binary float has no payload or sign on the wire (Section 6.2.4), although an engine can store distinct NaN bit patterns; every engine's own text and comparison treat them as one value.

- **Engine-assigned columns.** Some engine-assigned values cannot be written to a target of the same engine: a `rowversion`, a `COMPUTED` or `VIRTUAL` column, an `IDENTITY_ALWAYS` column where the target has no override, and a Db2 row-change timestamp or temporal period column. A consumer that cannot write such a value cannot reproduce it, and the target engine assigns its own. Identity defaults, sequence defaults and MySQL auto-update timestamps are writable and are reproduced. Appendix A says what a consumer does.

- **Byte stability of object forms.** The one-spelling rule holds for every string-valued form. The object-valued forms (interval, array shape, map, struct, range) fix member order and forbid whitespace, but a JSON library that re-serializes an event can reorder or re-space them. Byte comparison and hashing of a whole event are reliable only when the event is not re-serialized.

# Appendix A. Consumer Guidance (Informative)

Consumer behavior depends on the target. It is not a conformance subject. This appendix gives guidance at the SHOULD level, in the pattern of the Specification's Appendix A. Its keywords are advisory, as the keywords of that appendix are. The one consumer requirement that the Specification registers, C-TYPE-1 (decode by `logical_type`, never by `source_type`), is the Specification's.

- C-TYPE-2: A consumer SHOULD read the full descriptor, including every capability flag, before it decodes the first row of a column. A flag announces a value that the column can carry.

- C-TYPE-3: If the target of a consumer cannot hold a value at full fidelity, the consumer SHOULD raise an error or apply a conversion that the operator configured. It SHOULD NOT round, truncate, or substitute silently. This includes the special values `NaN`, an infinite date, a zero date, and `24:00:00`.

- C-TYPE-4: A consumer SHOULD treat a NATIVE value as an opaque string or byte sequence, unless it implements the named codec. A lakehouse target can store the value as such and record the codec name with it.

- C-TYPE-5: A consumer SHOULD treat a column with `listed: false` as mapped by the producing stream's own choice. It SHOULD read a NATIVE column of this kind only with the codec that the producing stream defines. It SHOULD NOT assume that another producer's stream maps or spells the same source type the same way.

- C-TYPE-6: A consumer SHOULD treat the `attributes` object as advisory. It changes neither the domain nor the decoding of a value.

- C-TYPE-7: A consumer that stores a NATIVE value as a string, in a target built for the string, SHOULD continue to do so if the descriptor of the column later changes to a family. The change arrives as a new OBJECT_METADATA. The consumer decides whether to migrate.

- C-TYPE-8: On decode of a stream whose wire protocol version is 0.3 or earlier, a consumer SHOULD accept the `Z` spelling of UTC and an unpadded fraction. Neither is conformant from the version this document applies to.

- C-TYPE-9: A consumer SHOULD compare `uuid` values by their 128 bits, not by the storage bytes of the engine. The wire spelling is the same for every engine.

- C-TYPE-10: A consumer that moves a SQL Server `DATETIME` column to a SQL Server target SHOULD map the written milliseconds back to the nearest 1/300-second tick. A round trip then reproduces the stored value.

- C-TYPE-11: A consumer that writes to the same engine SHOULD write the source value of every engine-assigned column that the target admits, so that keys and timestamps are preserved. That covers `IDENTITY_BY_DEFAULT`, `SEQUENCE` and `auto_update` columns (MySQL `ON UPDATE` timestamps can be assigned), and `IDENTITY_ALWAYS` columns where the target offers an override (SQL Server `IDENTITY_INSERT`, PostgreSQL and Db2 `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`). It SHOULD NOT write a `COMPUTED` or `VIRTUAL` column or a `rowversion`, which the target computes. Where a value cannot be preserved, the consumer SHOULD apply a conversion that the operator configures, not drop the value silently.

- C-TYPE-12: A consumer that applies a NATIVE `oracle.sdo_geometry.sdo@1` value to another engine SHOULD convert it as `SDO_UTIL.TO_WKTGEOMETRY` would. The element types WKT cannot express (arcs, optimized rectangles, solids, measures) SHOULD be a conversion that the operator configures.

- C-TYPE-13: A consumer that applies a `spatial` value to SQL Server SHOULD rewrite the OGC dimension markers into SQL Server's form, because SQL Server's WKT parser rejects the markers. `POINT Z (1 2 3)` becomes `POINT(1 2 3)`, and an absent Z before M becomes `NULL`.

# Change Log

- **v0.3**
  - Date: November 2026
  - Summary of Changes: Initial draft of the Type System on the family-and-trait model: nineteen families with domain traits and capability flags; the NATIVE tier with carrier and codec; the `attributes` object; the JSON binding with one grammar and inverse per value form; the type mapping dictionary for Oracle Database, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Db2, with seventeen NATIVE codecs; the tagged form for documents with native scalar types; requirements P-TYPE-1 to P-TYPE-10. Applies from the wire protocol version that follows 0.3.

# References

## Normative References

- **OpenCDC Specification Draft v0.7.0**
  - Role: Normative. Defines the CloudEvents envelope, the OBJECT_METADATA event that carries column descriptors (Specification Section 4), the DML value payload and the `_null_columns`, `_lob_overflow` and `_unavailable` fields (Section 5.2), the LOB obligations (Section 6.3), and the requirements register (Section 17). If this document and the Specification define the same field, the Specification governs the event and this document governs the type.

- **RFC 2119 -- Key Words for Use in RFCs**, as clarified by **RFC 8174**
  - Role: Normative. MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL carry the meanings defined therein, only when in upper case.

- **RFC 8259 -- The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format**
  - Role: Normative for the JSON binding (Section 6).

- **RFC 4648 -- The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings**
  - Role: Normative for byte values in the JSON binding (Section 6.10).

- **RFC 5234 -- Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF**, with **RFC 7405 -- Case-Sensitive String Support in ABNF**
  - Role: Normative. Section 6 writes the value grammars in ABNF. Every quoted string in those grammars is case-sensitive, as if it had the `%s` prefix of RFC 7405 (Section 6.1).

- **RFC 3339 -- Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps**
  - Role: Normative for the `T` separator and numeric offset profile of the temporal forms (Section 6.3).

- **ISO 8601-1:2019 -- Date and Time -- Representations for Information Interchange**
  - Role: Normative for the temporal forms, as restricted and extended in Section 6.3 (expanded year representation).

- **ECMA-262 -- ECMAScript Language Specification, 2024 edition, Number::toString**
  - Role: Normative for the spelling of binary floating-point values (Section 6.2.4).

- **RFC 9557 -- Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps with Additional Information**
  - Role: Normative for the time zone name suffix in Section 6.3.

- **RFC 9562 -- Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)**
  - Role: Normative for the uuid family.

- **IEEE 754-2019 -- Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic**
  - Role: Normative for the binary32, binary64, decimal64 and decimal128 formats named by the decimal family.

- **General Decimal Arithmetic Specification (Cowlishaw), Version 1.70, "to-scientific-string"**
  - Role: Normative for the VARIABLE_DECIMAL and DECIMAL_FLOAT forms.

- **OGC 06-103r4 -- Simple Feature Access, Part 1: Common Architecture, Version 1.2.1**
  - Role: Normative for Well-Known Text in the spatial family.

- **RFC 5952 -- A Recommendation for IPv6 Address Text Representation**
  - Role: Normative for the network family.
